newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Yachting: Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.
newsitem.headline: Australian Yachting: Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.

text.p: By Peter Campbell*
NO DOUBT, NO FEARR IS THE BEST
If an award is to be made for Yacht-of-the-Year, then it would have to go the Queensland-owned Farr 39, No Fearr, owned by young Townsville businessman CAREY RAMM.
No Fearr has won every IMS regatta it has contested since being launched last July.

She finished second in her division of the Sydney-Hobart and over the past two weeks finished first in her IMS division in Middle Harbour Yacht Club's Sydney-Mooloolaba race and first overall in Queensland Cruising Yacht Club's 49th Brisbane-Gladstone race.
No Fearr was designed by New Zealand's most successful yacht designer, BRUCE FARR, now based in the United States, and built in New Zealand by Cooksons.
She was set up here in Australia by PBS International, with RON JACOBS aboard for her most recent success the Brisbane-Gladstone race, and carries Fraser sails.

A fleet of 83 yachts started in the race to Gladstone, just one short of the fleet record, which augers well for a massive fleet entering for next year's 50th Brisbane-Gladstone. The 50th race will also draw from a big fleet heading north in the Sydney-Mooloolaba race the week before Easter.

In last weekend's Gladstone race, No Fearr won a hard-fought, tactical race up the Queensland coast in light to moderate south easterly breezes from the local yacht Restless, a modified Cape 35 skippered by RAY HOBBS, third place going to ATRIA, the 31-footer owned by Gold Coast heart surgeon GILBERT FORD and skippered by her designer ROBERT HICK from Melbourne.

Cruising Yacht Club of Australia director ROGER HICKMAN followed up his success with the DAVID LYONS-designed 43-footer ATARA in winning the CYCA's Blue Water Point Score for the 1996-97 season by placing a close fourth. In fact only less than 16 minutes separated the first five yachts on IMS corrected time with The Last Picasso (BOB ROBERTSON) placing fifth and BZW Challenge (RAY ROBERTS) sixth.

CYCA member PETER WALKER picked up the line honours double for both the Mooloolaba and Gladstone races with his revitalised KELL STEINMANN designed maxi Foxtel Amazon, although well outside the race record in both events. Foxtel Amazon is certainly going a lot faster with her new STEINMANN-designed keel, beating Exile in the race to Mooloolaba, Tower Life in the 308 nautical mile overnight dash to Gladstone.
BACARDI'S PORT FAIRY VICTORY

Sandringham Yacht Club Commodore, GRAEME AINLEY, steered his veteran sloop Bacardi to an all the way IMS corrected time win in Easter's Melbourne-Port Fairy race, the final event in the Ocean Racing Club of Victoria's summer season.
So good was the boat's performance in a race that saw five yachts retire, that if the rules had allowed, the PETERSON 43 could also have won the Performance Handicap division.

Bacardi led the fleet along Victoria's southwest coast for most of the 140 nautical mile race, with ROB HOPCRAFT's Animal Farm, an ADAMS 52, overtaking her only in the closing stages to take line honours by nine minutes.

Runner-up to Bacardi in the IMS division was JLW Chutzpah, skippered by Collins Street orthodontist BRUCE TAYLOR, a placing that was sufficient to give the HICK 35 the Ocean Racing Club's Summer Championship.
THREE PEAKS RACE TO COMPUTERLAND
The Boags Three Peaks Race has again proven it is one of the toughest races for sailor and landlubber.

Victory this year again went to Hobart medico, JOHN SAUL, skippering his Inglis 47, Computerland, but hero of the team was Hobart runner GERRY OLDFIELD, who kept them in the race by almost twice running the Flinders Island leg of 65 km, followed by a steep climb up Mt Strezlecki.

When OLDFIELD's running partner CHRIS FRENCH became ill at the base of the mountain, OLDFIELD volunteered to do the climb again, completing a total of 109 km, while FRENCH walked back to the little fishing port of Lady Barron to rejoin the yacht, fortunately recovering to complete the next two runs.
In addition to skipper JOHN SAUL and runners OLDFIELD and FRENCH, the crew of Computerland comprised Hobart sailors PETER FLETCHER and ROYCE SALTER.

The Three Peaks saw a fleet of monohulls and multihulls dash across Bass Strait, then combined offshore sailing with rugged mountain running, starting from Beauty Point on the Tamar River and ending on the Derwent River at Hobart, plus a dash up and down Mount Wellington which towers over Hobart.

On the way the yachts stopped at Lady Barron on Flinders Island and at Coles Bay on the Tasmanian East Coast to allow the runners on each boat to stretch their legs in cross-country runs and mountain climbs while the sailors relaxed.

The Three Peaks gets tremendous support from the small community on Flinders Island and it was appropriate that past winner RICHARD EDMUNDS should name his yacht Flinders Island Community for this year's race and then place second.
Third went to another Launceston yacht, Business Post, skippered by BRUCE GUY whose runners, Scotsmen ADRIAN DAVIS and JOHN COYLE, broke the records for the runs up Mt Freycinet and Mt Wellington.
SKIFF GRAND PRIX BECALMED

Sydney's 18-footer sailors have received a major set-back with the announcement by Grand Prix Sailing this week that it will not stage an 18-footer skiff circuit next season, instead concentrating its resources on an international circuit for the new Olympic 49er skiff class.

According to Bill McCartney, Grand Prix Sailing's founder and managing director, the World 49er class Council has awarded the rights to run six international events this year: two in Europe in June-July, two in the United States in July-August and two in Australia.
However, a rival promotional group is planning a 49-ers series for Australia and an announcement is expected next week.

Meanwhile, the 18-footer sailors, concerned at the lack of a national circuit and the effect it may have on the sponsorship of the sailing billboards are holding meetings to discuss setting up their own circuit.
The 18-footer circuit began in 1987 and has risen in profile as a result of the spectacular television coverage of grand prix races devised by McCartney.
18-FOOTER CHAMPION IN OLYMPIC BID

With the selection of the JULIAN BETHWAITE-designed 49er as the high-performance double-handed skiff for the Sydney 2000 Olympics, there was bound to be a defection from the ranks of the 18s, and it started right from the top last weekend.
World 18-footer champion CHRIS NICHOLSON and his crew DANIEL PHILLIPS made their 49-er debut with a brilliant victory in the Sail Sydney '97 regatta on Sydney Harbour.

NICHOLSON and PHILLIPS won eight of the 12 races in conditions that ranged from under eight knots to in excess of 25 knots over the Easter weekend, easily winning the series from EMMETT LAZICH and MICHAEL SHANE.
More than 200 sailors from all Australian States, New Zealand, Russia, Singapore and The Netherlands contested the regatta which saw Sydney Harbour in Olympic mode for a most successful series.

Although struggling in their earlier races, our Savannah Olympians came good at the end, with the Tornado catamarans class going to silver medallist MITCH BOOTH and his crew ADAM BEASHEL, the Victorians TOM KING and MARK TURNBULL winning the 470s and PAUL McKENZIE, also from Melbourne, winning the Finn single-handed class.

In the Soling keelboats, Star class bronze medallists at Savannah COLIN BEASHEL and DAVID GILES were joined by Barcelona Olympian MICHAEL MOTTLE to tie for first place with match-racing helmsman NEVILLE WITTEY with his crew of DAVID EDWARDS and JOSHUA GRACE.

MICHAEL MOTTLE flew in from the United States last week not only to sail in the Solings at Sail Sydney but also with a family reunion with father GEORGE back in Sydney for a visit after living for several years in his native Czechoslovakia.
GEORGE MOTTLE also made a comeback to ocean racing, sailing to Mooloolaba with Middle Harbour yachtsman JOHN WALKER aboard Impeccable.
APRIL FOOLS DAY REPORTS
Browsing the April 1 edition of the International Sailing Federation's web page we came across the following information:
DENNIS CONNER, who weighs in at around 136 kilos, has announced his America's Cup challenge with primary sponsorship provided by Sarah Ferguson's employer, Weight Watchers.

International Sailing Federation president and Canada's favourite sailing son with a shining dome, PAUL HENDERSON, will helm a Mumm 36 in this year's Champagne Mumm Admiral's Cup with sponsorship from Pharmacia and Upjohn Inc, a multinational drug company whose products include Rogaine Hair Regrowth Treatment for men and women with common hereditary hair loss.
* Peter Campbell is editor of OFFSHORE Yachting magazine. -- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800.
